932.title: The Salvation Army
932.hook: William and Catherine Booth take soup, soap and salvation into the streets of London's East End
932.howItsDone: Salvation Army corps hold Sunday worship with brass bands and run food banks, shelters and recovery programs, and its officers serve as both ministers and social workers.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Spurgeon, who told his students the truth about his own dark days. Your line was even preachers get low.

A drum, then a cornet, then a few voices singing, off key and loud, on a street corner in the East End of London, outside a pub. People stop, some to listen, some to jeer. The singers wear uniforms. Their leader is called the General. If it sounds like an army, that's the point: a church that decided to march into the poor streets instead of waiting for the poor to come to church. It was started by a preacher named William Booth and his wife, Catherine, a preacher too. Today, a church with brass bands, ranks, and a pot of soup on the stove.

The Booths' work began as the Christian Mission. The story goes that a report described it as a volunteer army, and William crossed out volunteer and wrote salvation. However it happened, the name stuck, and so did the ranks and uniforms. Catherine didn't stand behind her husband. She preached to crowds herself, and wrote in defense of women preaching, when women in the pulpit were hotly argued over. The Army gave women real leadership from its early days. The Army became known by a short phrase: soup, soap, salvation. Feed people. Help them get clean, find a bed, find work. And tell them about the love of God. Soup comes first: hungry people can't hear much. The Booths could point to Isaiah, where God describes the fast he wants, in the King James Bible: "Is it not to deal thy bread to the hungry, and that thou bring the poor that are cast out to thy house?" The Salvation Army is a church in its own right, with its own officers as ministers. Salvationists don't hold baptism or communion services; they say the inner grace those rites point to is what counts, and they live it out in service. Catholic and Orthodox churches, and Protestant churches such as Lutherans and Anglicans, hold those rites at the very center of their life. Both sides say so openly, and the Army works alongside other churches. And salvation itself? In the Greek of the New Testament, it can mean rescue, safety and health, not only heaven. Soup, soap and salvation are three parts of one rescue.

Picture the nearest place that feeds or shelters people, a food bank, a shelter, a church pantry, and then your own shelf: a can of soup, a bar of soap, a toothbrush still in its packet. Choose one thing to set aside, and hold in mind the person who will open it. If you pray, pray for them.
William Booth. The preacher who, with his wife Catherine, founded the Salvation Army and crossed out volunteer for salvation in its name.
Your line: soup, soap, salvation. Sometimes the simplest need comes first. Day nine hundred thirty-two, done.

933.title: Hudson Taylor
933.hook: an English missionary in China puts on Chinese clothes, grows the braid, and learns the dialects
933.howItsDone: Some Christian mission agencies today ask workers to learn the local language and culture deeply before anything else, and churches in China are led by Chinese Christians.

segments.voice: Yesterday: William Booth's Salvation Army, its brass bands, its uniforms and its pot of soup. Your line was soup, soap, salvation.

A barber's razor scrapes across the front of a young Englishman's head. The hair at the back is left to grow, so it can be braided into a long queue, the way Chinese men wore it then. He folds away his European suit and puts on the loose robe and cloth shoes of a Chinese teacher. Other foreigners in the port city laugh at him. Some missionaries are embarrassed for him. A few are angry: he's letting the side down. His name is Hudson Taylor, and if he's going to live among the people of China, he's going to stop looking like a visitor.

The first change was the map. Taylor wanted to go beyond the port cities, inland, to provinces far from the sea. So he founded the China Inland Mission, and asked those who joined to dress as he did, learn the local dialects, and live simply among their neighbors. The reason he gave was Paul, in the King James Bible: "I am made all things to all men, that I might by all means save some." Taylor applied it to his wardrobe. If a foreign suit was a wall, he would take it off. Christians say God did this first. John's Gospel says: "And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us." In Christian belief, God didn't shout from a distance; he came close, in a body, a language, a place. Some readers see Taylor's clothes and dialects as a small echo of that. Then the harder part, from day nine hundred seventeen and Ramabai: the honest history of missions. Taylor came to China in an age of empire, when Western powers had used force to open China's ports, and opium was part of that trade. Taylor spoke out against the opium trade, and wanted the gospel to look Chinese rather than British. But he was still a foreigner, and the clothes didn't change that. In time, Chinese Christians led their own churches, and they hold a range of views about the missionary era. The idea Taylor reached for was simple and costly: don't ask people to become like you. Become one of them, as far as love can take you.

934.title: Amy Carmichael
934.hook: in south India, a missionary opens her home to girls at risk of exploitation and writes of love that costs
934.howItsDone: Amy Carmichael's books are read for devotion by some Christians, and the household she founded at Dohnavur continues as a community led by Indian Christians.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Hudson Taylor, who folded away his suit and went inland. Your line was become one of them.

Early one morning, a little girl stands at the door of a mission house in south India. She has run away in the night. The story told about her, by the woman who opened the door, is that she had been given to a temple as a small child, and she was afraid of what was coming. Her name, in that story, is Preena. The woman at the door is Amy Carmichael, a missionary from Ireland who wears a sari and works alongside Indian women. She takes the child in. The people who claim the girl come to get her back. Amy doesn't hand her over.

Through that child and others, Carmichael learned of a custom in parts of India by which some girls were given to temples as children, and some were sexually exploited as they grew. She wasn't the only one to oppose it. Indian reformers, Hindu and Christian, campaigned against the practice too, and Indian law later banned it. Carmichael's part was a home. It grew into a large household at a place called Dohnavur, later including boys as well. The children called her Amma, mother. Indian coworkers ran much of it beside her. She wanted it to be a family, not an institution. That home had a price. Taking children in made her enemies and brought her trouble. She gave up comfort, home leave, and a life anyone in Ireland would have recognized. In her poems and books she wrote about love that costs: love that gives up nothing, she said, isn't really love. The first letter of John says something close, in the King James Bible: "My little children, let us not love in word, neither in tongue; but in deed and in truth." Deed and truth: love you can see by what it gives up. Looking back, some Christians remember her with deep gratitude, and some also ask hard questions about the mission era she worked in. Neither takes away the girl at the door, or the door that stayed open.

Bring to mind a child in your life, your own, a niece, a neighbor's kid, a student, and ask quietly: is there one thing I could do to make this child safer, or to be an adult they could tell if something were wrong? Maybe closer attention, or simply being someone steady; if you're ever worried a child is in danger, the protecting step is to call the people whose job it is. If you pray, hold that child before God by name.
Amy Carmichael. A missionary in south India who opened her home to girls at risk, and became Amma to a household of children.
Your line: love that costs. Real love usually gives up something: time, comfort or pride. That's day nine hundred thirty-four.

935.title: Bernadette
935.hook: Catholics tell of a poor, sickly girl at Lourdes to whom Mary appeared, and of a spring the sick still come to
935.howItsDone: Catholic pilgrims travel to Lourdes to pray at the grotto, join candlelight processions and bathe in the spring water, and the sick are brought there with volunteers who help care for them.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Amy Carmichael, and a girl at the door who wasn't handed back. Your line was love that costs.

Cold water, a riverbank, a girl gathering firewood and bones to sell. That's how the story begins, as Catholics tell it. Her name is Bernadette Soubirous. Her family is poor enough to be living in a former jail cell in Lourdes, in the south of France. She is small, often sick, and can barely read. Near a rocky hollow by the river, a grotto, she says she sees a lady dressed in white, with a rosary. Nobody else sees anything. Her mother is worried, the town curious, the police suspicious. Bernadette keeps going back.
screen: `A LADY IN WHITE IN THE GROTTO.`

segments.voice: The spring comes first. In Bernadette's account, the lady told her to drink from the spring and wash in it. There was no spring she could see. So she dug in the muddy ground with her hands, and the crowd thought she had lost her mind. Then water began to flow, and it still flows. Then the name. For a long time the lady didn't say who she was. When Bernadette finally asked, she reported the answer in her local dialect: I am the Immaculate Conception. She said she didn't know what the words meant, and repeated them all the way to the priest so she wouldn't forget. In Catholic teaching, the Immaculate Conception means Mary was kept free from original sin from the moment her life began. Here the churches differ. The Catholic Church investigated, and judged that the appearances could be believed. It also teaches that no Catholic is required to believe in private revelations like this one. Orthodox Christians honor Mary deeply, but describe her holiness in their own terms. Protestant churches don't treat visions like this as part of their teaching. And Bernadette? She didn't stay to be famous. She became a nun, far from Lourdes, often ill, and the Catholic Church later named her a saint. At the spring, the sick are brought to pray and to bathe, and the Church examines claims of healing carefully. Christians in other churches pray for the sick too, as the letter of James describes, in the King James Bible: "Is any sick among you? let him call for the elders of the church; and let them pray over him."

Bring to mind one person who is sick right now, and picture them, not their illness, them. Then add someone sick whom nobody is praying for, a stranger in a ward somewhere. If you pray, hold them both before God, or, if it's your way, ask Mary to pray for them; if you don't, simply wish them strength.
Bernadette. A poor, sickly girl from Lourdes who said Mary appeared to her at a grotto, and who dug in the mud until water came.
Your line: the spring at the grotto. It began with a girl digging in mud. See you tomorrow.

936.title: The little way
936.hook: Thérèse of Lisieux finds holiness in small things done with great love
936.howItsDone: Catholics keep Thérèse's feast day and read Story of a Soul, and some Christians take up her little way by offering ordinary tasks and small kindnesses to God through the day.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Bernadette, digging in the mud at Lourdes until water came. Your line was the spring at the grotto.

Dirty water keeps landing on a young nun's face. She's at the laundry tubs in a convent in Lisieux, in France, and the sister beside her is scrubbing so hard the spray flies every time. The young nun wants to step back and wipe her face. Instead, she decides to stand there and take it as a small gift. She tells it herself, in her memoir. It's not a dramatic story. That's the point. Her name is Thérèse, and she spent the rest of her short life inside those convent walls, finding a way to God made of moments like this. Today, the little way.

Thérèse read about the great saints and felt like a grain of sand next to a mountain. In her memoir, later published as Story of a Soul, she says she was too small to climb the steep stairway of perfection. So she looked for another way up. She lived in a time of new inventions, and she pictured an elevator: something that carries you up when you can't climb. She found it in two lines of scripture. Proverbs, in the Catholic Douay-Rheims Bible: "Whosoever is a little one, let him come to me." And Isaiah: "As one whom the mother caresseth, so will I comfort you." The lift, she decided, was being carried: not climbing harder, but staying small and letting God's arms do the lifting. Jesus says something close in Matthew, in the King James Bible: "Except ye be converted, and become as little children, ye shall not enter into the kingdom of heaven." In a day, it looked like this. A smile for a sister who got on her nerves. Not answering back. Letting the water hit her face. Doing the dull job carefully. She described these as flowers she could scatter, small things no one would notice, done with as much love as she could put into them. Thérèse died young, inside the same convent. The Catholic Church later named her a saint and a Doctor of the Church, a title for teachers whose writing is trusted to guide the whole Church. Christians outside the Catholic Church read her book too, and find laundry tubs, chores and small kindnesses.

Look for the smallest, dullest job in your day: folding laundry, a reply to an email, listening to a story you've heard before. Picture doing it slowly and carefully, as if for someone you love, knowing probably no one will see. If you pray, offer it to God before you start, the way Thérèse did.
Lisieux. The French convent town where a young nun found God not by climbing higher but by staying small, in laundry tubs and hidden kindnesses.
Your line: small things, great love. Nobody has to notice for it to count. That's day nine hundred thirty-six.

937.title: Damien of Molokai
937.hook: a priest goes to a settlement for people with leprosy, and one day begins his sermon, we lepers
937.howItsDone: Catholics keep Saint Damien's feast and pray for people with Hansen's disease and for those who care for them, and Christians of other churches also tell his story when they talk about serving people pushed to the margins.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Thérèse of Lisieux and her little way: no great deeds, just small things done with great love.

Boats struggle to land at this beach. Cliffs stand behind it like a wall, the sea in front is rough, and people are put ashore however the crew can manage. Once they're here, they don't leave. This strip of the Hawaiian island of Molokai is where the kingdom sent people with leprosy, now called Hansen's disease, to keep them away from everyone else. Families said goodbye on the dock in Honolulu. A young Belgian priest, Father Damien, offers to go. He builds houses, digs graves, dresses sores, plays with the children. And one Sunday, tradition says, he changes a single word.

Damien had preached to the settlement the way an outsider would. You. Your suffering. Your hope. Then he noticed the signs of the disease on his own body. He had caught it. The story told about the next Sunday is short: he began his sermon with two words, we lepers. Not you. We. That word is the whole lesson. Plenty of people helped the settlement from a safe distance. Damien was now inside it, with no way back out, and the people he served, the story goes, heard the difference. Behind it is a scene in Mark. A man with leprosy kneels before Jesus: if you want to, you can make me clean. In the King James Bible: "And Jesus, moved with compassion, put forth his hand, and touched him." The law of the time kept people with that disease apart, and the story stops to say Jesus reached out a hand before he said a word. Hebrews says of Jesus and the people he came for: "he is not ashamed to call them brethren." Some Christians read Damien's life as that sentence, lived out on a beach. He kept working after the diagnosis, and the disease took his life on Molokai. The Catholic Church names him a saint, and Christians of other churches honor him too. One honest note. Some of the people sent to Molokai would rather not be called lepers at all; it names a person by a disease. Damien could say the word only because he'd become one of them. The lesson isn't the label. It's the we.

Name, quietly, a group people talk about as they: the unhoused man on the corner, the kid nobody sits with, people with an illness others fear. Then try the word we instead: we who get sick, we who get left out, we who need a hand. If you pray, pray for them as we; if you don't, just let the we sit there.
Damien. The priest who went to live with people sent away for leprosy on Molokai, caught the disease himself, and began preaching, we lepers.
Your line: we lepers. Not you, but we, said from the inside. See you tomorrow.

938.title: Charles de Foucauld
938.hook: a soldier turned hermit lives among the Tuareg in the Sahara as a brother to all
938.howItsDone: Small communities of laypeople, priests and religious sisters inspired by Charles de Foucauld live simply among poor neighbors, working ordinary jobs and keeping a time of quiet prayer each day.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Damien of Molokai, who caught the disease and began his sermon, we lepers.

A young French cavalry officer throws parties, runs up debts, and gets disciplined for bringing a mistress along on a posting to North Africa. Faith means nothing to him. Years later the same man lives in a small hut deep in the Sahara, with a notebook of words in the language of the Tuareg, the desert people around him, and a chapel the size of a closet. He doesn't preach on street corners or run a school. Mostly, he's just there, with his door open.

Back in the faith as a young man, Charles de Foucauld looked for the plainest life he could find. He tried a monastery, and left it for something even smaller. What drew him was the part of Jesus's life the Gospels barely describe: the quiet years in Nazareth. Luke gives them two verses. In the King James Bible: "And he went down with them, and came to Nazareth, and was subject unto them." No sermons, no miracles, just a household. That hidden life, Foucauld decided, was a way to follow Jesus too. So he went into the desert to be a neighbor. He learned Tuareg well enough to gather their poems and write down their words. He gave out medicine and grain and sat with whoever came by. He wrote that he wanted everyone around him, Christian, Muslim, Jewish or anyone else, to see him as a brother, a universal brother, and he called his little house the fraternity. In Luke, a lawyer asks Jesus who his neighbor is. Jesus tells of a Samaritan who stops for a beaten stranger, then turns the question around: "Which now of these three, thinkest thou, was neighbour unto him that fell among the thieves?" Some readers hear Foucauld's life as an answer. He built no large church. He died at his own door during a raid. But others later formed communities inspired by him, small groups who live and work among the poor, and the Catholic Church has named him a saint. This week: soup, soap and salvation in the East End. Hudson Taylor in Chinese clothes. Amy Carmichael's love that costs. The spring at the grotto. Small things, great love. We lepers. And a brother in the desert. Seven stories, one direction: closer.

Picture one person near you who isn't family and isn't quite a friend: a coworker, a neighbor, the person who cleans your building. Foucauld's whole method was attention: a language learned, a door open, time given. If you pray, pray for them by name; if not, give them a minute of that attention.
Foucauld. A French cavalry officer turned hermit in the Sahara, who wanted everyone around him, Christian, Muslim or Jewish, to call him brother.
Your line: universal brother. A door left open to everyone. A week of moving closer, done.

chat.says: What did Charles de Foucauld actually do out in the desert? Did he preach a lot?
options: He mostly just lived as a neighbor: learned their language, gave medicine, kept his door open.
He built a big mission church there and ran a school to convert the Tuareg.
He lived alone in silence, cut off from everyone, praying day and night in his chapel.
chat.meaning: Foucauld followed Jesus's hidden Nazareth years: no big church, just being a universal brother, a language learned and a door open.
